title: Mircea Gherghina
text:
I am a Postdoctoral Research Associate at the Watson School of International and Public Affairs at Brown University, where I am part of the Climate Solutions Lab. I received my PhD in Sociology from the University of Toronto.
My current work follows two lines. The first looks at inequalities in distributive environmental policies and green markets, including household adoption of solar PV in Connecticut and New York; at Brown, I am extending this to how climate risks shape community resilience and energy behavior. The second, which grew out of my dissertation, asks how emerging climate technologies such as carbon capture gain political support despite uncertain outcomes, and how stakeholder representation in U.S. Senate energy hearings has changed over two decades. I combine computational text analysis with interviews, including with carbon capture entrepreneurs.
Before academia, I worked at the European Central Bank and as a freelance researcher. I hold an MSc in Social Science Research Methods from the University of Bristol and an undergraduate degree in economics from the Bucharest University of Economic Studies.

title: Mircea Gherghina
text:
Course instructor

Energy, Climate and Society (IAPA 1700G) Brown University, Spring and Fall 2026






Course description





This course examines the social side of how energy is produced and used. It begins with fossil fuels and their effects on communities and the environment, then turns to energy transitions and the social forces that help or hold back renewable energy. A central question runs throughout: who benefits from energy change, and who bears its costs? Students build policy analysis skills by identifying energy challenges, assessing their social impacts, and proposing evidence-based solutions.





Social Data Analytics (CCT 416) University of Toronto, Winter 2024
Syllabus






Course description





A lab-based course on collecting and analyzing social data, for beginning and intermediate researchers. Students read recent “big data” studies and discuss their theory, critiques, and ethics, while learning Python programming, web scraping, data collection and storage, basic statistics, and data visualization. The course ends with a research project on a topic of each student’s choice.
